questions.question: The parliamentary standing committees have a tenure of ________ years.
questions.solution: Most parliamentary standing committees (such as the department-related standing committees) have a tenure of one year. After this period, the committees are reconstituted. Note: This ensures that a wide range of Members of Parliament get the opportunity to participate in the legislative and oversight process over time.

questions.question: Which of the following Fundamental Rights is available for Indians as well as foreigners?
questions.option_2: Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
questions.option_3: Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
questions.option_4: Right to protection of language, script and culture of minorities
questions.solution: The Right to elementary education (Article 21A) is a Fundamental Right available to both Indians and foreigners. Contrast: Certain rights, such as Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 (which include minority rights and public employment opportunities), are exclusively reserved for citizens of India only.

questions.question: How many types of writs can be issued by the Supreme Court to protect the Fundamental Rights of Indian citizens?
questions.solution: The Supreme Court can issue five types of writs under Article 32 to protect the Fundamental Rights of citizens. These are Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-Warranto. Role: These writs are the primary tools for the 'Right to Constitutional Remedies,' ensuring that rights are not just on paper but enforceable.

questions.question: Which committee is related to fundamental duties?
questions.solution: The Verma Committee (1999) is related to Fundamental Duties; it was tasked with identifying legal provisions for the implementation of these duties. Note: While the Swaran Singh Committee recommended their inclusion, the Verma Committee focused on the practical and legal frameworks surrounding them.

questions.question:
A housemaid gets her 12-year-old daughter to help in her work as a house cleaner at a residential colony instead of sending her to school.

Which fundamental duty is violated by the housemaid?
questions.option_1: To provide opportunities for education to his/her child
questions.option_2: To defend the country and render national service
questions.option_3: To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood
questions.option_4: To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
questions.solution: By choosing work over schooling for a child, the fundamental duty to provide opportunities for education to one's child or ward between the ages of 6 and 14 is violated. This duty (Article 51A[k]) was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 to complement the fundamental right to education.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of Directive Principles of State Policy, and also distinguishes it from Fundamental Rights?
questions.option_4: It protects the interest of the individual.
questions.solution: The most significant feature that distinguishes Directive Principles (DPSP) from Fundamental Rights is that they are non-justiciable. This means that unlike Fundamental Rights, citizens cannot approach a court for their legal enforcement if the State fails to implement them. They are moral and political obligations of the State.

questions.question:
All historical monuments have signages with instructions that public should not write on the walls.

To which fundamental duty does the given statement belong?
questions.option_2: To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
questions.option_3: To promote harmony and spirit of common brotherhood
questions.option_4: To defend the country and render national service
questions.solution: Instructions against writing on walls or damaging monuments relate to the fundamental duty to safeguard public property and to abjure violence (Article 51A[i]). Note: While Article 49 makes it a State duty to protect monuments, Article 51A makes it a civic duty for every individual citizen.

questions.question: The Fundamental Duties of Citizens were introduced by the 42nd Amendment in the year:
questions.solution: The Fundamental Duties were introduced into the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act in 1976. This amendment added Part IV-A and Article 51A to the Constitution, based on the context of the internal emergency prevailing at the time.

questions.question: On 26 January 1950 India became:
questions.solution: On 26 January 1950, the Preamble of the Constitution officially declared India to be a Sovereign, Democratic, Republic. Context: The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were not in the original 1950 Preamble; they were added later via the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

questions.question: How is the structure of health infrastructure and health care system in India?
questions.solution: The public healthcare system in India is organized as a three-tier system. This includes Primary (Sub-centers and PHCs), Secondary (Community Health Centers and District Hospitals), and Tertiary (Specialized hospitals and Medical Colleges). This structure aims to provide a referral chain from rural areas to specialized centers.

questions.question: Which Section of the Representation of People’s Act (RPA), 1951 deprives the prisoners of their right to vote?
questions.solution: Section 62 (5) of the Representation of the People Act (RPA), 1951 specifies that no person shall vote at any election if he is confined in a prison, whether under a sentence of imprisonment or transportation or otherwise, or is in the lawful custody of the police. Exception: This does not apply to persons subjected to preventive detention.

questions.question: The Citizenship Act, 1955 does NOT deal with ____________.
questions.solution: The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides for the acquisition, termination, and determination of citizenship in India. It does NOT deal with elections, which are governed by other laws like the Representation of the People Acts and provisions under Part XV of the Constitution.

questions.question: Which of the following writs in Latin means ‘we command’?
questions.solution: The writ of Mandamus literally means 'we command' in Latin. It is issued by a superior court to a public official, public body, corporation, inferior court, or the government, commanding them to perform a legal duty that they have failed or refused to perform.

questions.question: A ________ is issued to prevent an inferior court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction, which is not legally vested, or acting without jurisdiction or acting against the principles of natural justice.
questions.solution: The writ of prohibition is issued to prevent an inferior court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction or acting against the principles of natural justice. Distinction: While Certiorari is issued to quash an order after a decision is made, Prohibition is issued while the proceedings are pending to stop the court from proceeding further.

questions.question: Which writ literally means 'what is your authority’?
questions.solution: The writ of Quo-Warranto literally means 'by what authority' or 'what is your authority.' It is issued by the court to enquire into the legality of the claim of a person to a public office, preventing the illegal usurpation of a public office by an individual.

questions.question: Citizens are NOT discriminated against on the basis of religion, caste or sex because of:
questions.solution: Non-discrimination on the basis of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth is a core component of the Right to Equality (specifically Article 15). It ensures that all citizens have equal standing in the eyes of the State regarding access to public spaces and services.

questions.question: Which of the following organisations said that India CANNOT have a parallel judicial system - one for the rich and the other for the poor?
questions.solution: The Supreme Court of India has repeatedly emphasized that the rule of law implies equality before the law, stating that India cannot have a parallel judicial system—one for the rich and another for the poor. This underscores the importance of legal aid and fair trial for every citizen regardless of status.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a way to acquire citizenship in India?
questions.solution: Renunciation is a way to lose or terminate citizenship, not acquire it. The Citizenship Act, 1955 specifies five ways to acquire citizenship: Birth, Descent, Registration, Naturalization, and Incorporation of Territory.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a condition for acquiring the citizenship of India?
questions.solution: Holding property is NOT a condition for acquiring Indian citizenship. Citizenship in India is based on legal principles like birth, descent, and registration, and is entirely independent of an individual's wealth or property ownership.

questions.question: Any citizen of India can make a declaration renouncing his/her Indian citizenship under the ________.
questions.solution: The Citizenship Act, 1955 is the primary legislation that allows a citizen of India of full age and capacity to make a declaration renouncing their Indian citizenship. Upon registration of such a declaration, that person ceases to be a citizen of India.

questions.question: Which of the following Sections of the Indian Penal Code deals with 'rape'?
questions.solution: Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) defines the offense of rape and lists the circumstances that constitute the crime. Update: Under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which replaces the IPC, these provisions have been reorganized into new sections.

questions.question: The Press and Registration of Books (PRB) Act was enacted in which year?
questions.solution: The Press and Registration of Books (PRB) Act was enacted in 1867. It was a colonial-era law designed to regulate printing presses and the registration of books and newspapers, ensuring the government could keep a record of all published materials.
